library(DDMethods)

General Growth Balance (GGB)

This vignette describes the methods for the General Growth Balance Death Distribution Method (DDM) for estimating completeness of death registration. These methods are not original to this package, but are summarized here. For original sources, see the references section of this vignette.

Input data

Input data required for GGB is:

  • Age-specific population counts from two censuses (recommended < 20 years apart)
  • Age-specific death counts from death registration in between the two censuses

Age-specific death counts can come from one or many years of death registration, but should be converted to average annual counts.

This package includes an example dataset, which matches the example used but the IUSSP.

The example dataset is for South African males, between 2001 and 2007:

head(zaf_2001_2007)
#>        location    pop1    pop2    deaths  migrants age_start    sex      date1
#>          <char>   <num>   <num>     <num>     <num>     <num> <char>     <Date>
#> 1: South Africa 2223006 2505744 197911.88 10605.138         0   male 2001-10-10
#> 2: South Africa 2425066 2560642  15566.49  2848.486         5   male 2001-10-10
#> 3: South Africa 2518985 2452339  11207.11  5152.799        10   male 2001-10-10
#> 4: South Africa 2453156 2553293  25472.64 16573.504        15   male 2001-10-10
#> 5: South Africa 2099417 2362519  54959.64 14802.771        20   male 2001-10-10
#> 6: South Africa 1899275 2033165 102802.12  4714.013        25   male 2001-10-10
#>         date2
#>        <Date>
#> 1: 2007-02-15
#> 2: 2007-02-15
#> 3: 2007-02-15
#> 4: 2007-02-15
#> 5: 2007-02-15
#> 6: 2007-02-15

As-is, these data are for total deaths in the interval, so we need to divide deaths by the time between censuses in years. Note that in the ggb function, this happens internally, via the input_deaths_annual argument.

# convert to average annual values
dt <- copy(zaf_2001_2007)
dt[, t := as.numeric(difftime(date2, date1, units = "days")) / 365]
dt[, deaths := deaths / t]
dt[, migrants := migrants / t]

The Demographic Balancing Equation

At the core of the GGB method is the demographics balancing equation, which says that in a stable population (constant birth rate and age-specific mortality rate over time), population growth rate (rr) is equal to birth rate (bb) minus death rate (dd) plus migration rate (mm). In a closed population, this simplifies to: r=b−dr = b - d.

This base form of the demographic balancing equation looks at all ages and uses birth rate as the entry rate into the population. But, we can think of an analogous format for any age aa, where “births” become birthdays at age aa and the population of interest is the population aged a+a+. Then, r(a+)=b(a+)−d(a+)r(a+) = b(a+) - d(a+).

From two censuses, we can approximate r(a+)r(a+) and b(a+)b(a+) for a collection of ages aa. True death rate, d(a+)d(a+), itself is a function of observed death count, observed population counts, death registration completeness, and census coverage. We leverage these relationships, along with orthogonal regression to summarize across ages, to estimate completeness. The following sections will describe each component in more detail.

A bit on notation

As described, we notate r(a+)r(a+), b(a+)b(a+), d(a+)d(a+), and m(a+)m(a+) to be the growth, birth (or entry), death, and migration rates in the population aged aa and over.

Additionally:

  • nn : length of age interval in data
  • N1N1 : population at census 1
  • N2N2 : population at census 2
  • NN : mean population between census 1 and census 2
  • DD : average annual deaths recorded between censuses

And we use traditional demographic notation where nZx{_nZ_x} stands for some demographic measure, ZZ, for the age interval xx to x+nx+n.

Entry rate, b(a+)

We can estimate the entry rate into the population age a+a+ such that: b(a+)=birthdays aged aN(a+)b(a+) = \frac{\text{birthdays aged } a}{N(a+)} Where average annual birthdays aged aa is approximated as the geometric mean of nN1a−n{_nN1_{a-n}} and nN2a{_nN2_a} divided by the length of the age interval (nn): birthdays aged a=1nnN1a−n⋅nN2a\text{birthdays aged } a = \frac{1}{n}\sqrt{{_nN1_{a-n}} \cdot {_nN2_a}} And N(a+)N(a+) is approximated as the geometric mean of N1(a+)N1(a+) and N2(a+)N2(a+): N(a+)=N1(a+)⋅N2(a+)N(a+) = \sqrt{N1(a+) \cdot N2(a+)} Note that if we assume census coverage is the same for all age groups, coverage does not impact this entry rate term. This is because a coverage scalar applied to N1N1 and N2N2 would cancel in the numerator and denominator when we divide birthdays by N(a+)N(a+).

On our example dataset, we get:

Growth rate, r(a+)

The growth rate can be approximated as:

r(a+)=1tln(N2(a+)N1(a+))r(a+) = \frac{1}{t} \text{ln} \Bigg(\frac{N2(a+)}{N1(a+)}\Bigg) Alternatively, it can be approximated as:

r(a+)=1t⋅N2(a+)−N1(a+)N(a+)r(a+) = \frac{1}{t} \cdot \frac{N2(a+) - N1(a+)} {N(a+)} with N(a+)N(a+) computed as it is described above.

The first method for estimating growth rate comes from Hill, You, and Choi (2009). The second is used by IUSSP and Tim Riffe’s DDM package.

Now, consider the case where census 1 and census 2 have coverage k1k1 and k2k2 such that true populations are N1(a+)k1\frac{N1(a+)}{k1} and N2(a+)k2\frac{N2(a+)}{k2}. Coverage is assumed to be the same for all age groups. Let r(a+)r(a+) be growth rate as estimated in the first equation above, and let r(a+)′r(a+)' be growth rate that incorporates k1k1 and k2k2. Using the first growth equation, we get: r(a+)′=1tln(N2(a+)/k2N1(a+)/k1)r(a+)' = \frac{1}{t} \text{ln} \Bigg(\frac{N2(a+) / k2}{N1(a+) / k1}\Bigg) when we apply coverage scalars to the observed NN values.

With some algebra, we can get:

⟹r(a+)′=1t(ln(N2(a+)N1(a+))+ln(k1k2)) \implies r(a+)' = \frac{1}{t} \Bigg( \text{ln} \Bigg(\frac{N2(a+)}{N1(a+)} \Bigg) + \text{ln}\Big(\frac{k1}{k2} \Big)\Bigg) ⟹r(a+)′=r(a+)+δ where δ=1tln(k1k2) \implies r(a+)' = r(a+) + \delta \text{ where } \delta = \frac{1}{t}\text{ln}\big(\frac{k1}{k2}\big) and we can think of δ\delta here as the error in growth rate when estimated using N2(a+)N2(a+) and N1(a+)N1(a+). We will use this δ\delta later in the demographic balancing equation.

In our example dataset, we find growth rate (r(a+)r(a+)) to be:

#>     age_start    pop1       pop2    deaths growth_rate
#>         <num>   <num>      <num>     <num>       <num>

#>  2:         5 2425066 2560641.90  2907.763  0.01522950

#>  6:        25 1899275 2033165.30 19203.056  0.02175217

#> 15:        70  232604  241976.30 13642.915  0.02002466

Death rate, d(a+)

Given that death rate is by definition deaths over person-years, we can get an incomplete death rate as follows:

d(a+)=D(a+)N(a+)d(a+) = \frac{D(a+)}{N(a+)}

where the numerator is deaths from the data and the denominator is population as estimated above.

When death registration is incomplete, true deaths are D(a+)c\frac{D(a+)}{c} where cc is death registration completeness. Additionally, the denominator N(a+)N(a+) is estimated from the two censuses and may be biased if one census has higher coverage.

To estimate this bias from censuses, we’ll go back to how we estimated N(a+)N(a+), apply k1k1 and k2k2 scalars to census 1 and census 2, and see how that modifies our population estimate. Let N(a+)′N(a+)' be a version of population that accounts for k1k1 and k2k2 and N(a+)N(a+) remain population as estimated above. So:

N(a+)′=N1(a+)⋅N2(a+)k1⋅k2N(a+)' = \sqrt{\frac{N1(a+) \cdot N2(a+)}{k1 \cdot k2}}

⟹N(a+)′=(N1(a+)⋅N2(a+))(1k1⋅k2) \implies N(a+)' = \Big(\sqrt{N1(a+) \cdot N2(a+)} \Big) \Big(\sqrt{\frac{1}{k1 \cdot k2}} \Big)

⟹N(a+)′=N(a+)⋅1k1⋅k2 \implies N(a+)' = N(a+) \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{k1 \cdot k2}}

Next, go back to the formulation of d(a+)d(a+). Substitute D(a+)c\frac{D(a+)}{c} for the numerator and substitute N(a+)′N(a+)' for N(a+)N(a+) in the denominator. Doing this, we get:

d(a+)=D(a+)cN(a+)(k1⋅k2)12d(a+) = \frac{\frac{D(a+)}{c}}{\frac{N(a+)}{(k1 \cdot k2) ^ \frac{1}{2}}}

⟹d(a+)=(k1⋅k2)12c⋅D(a+)N(a+) \implies d(a+) = \frac{(k1 \cdot k2) ^ \frac{1}{2}}{c} \cdot \frac{D(a+)}{N(a+)}

Regression to estimate completeness

Putting this together by using the balancing equation, and error components for growth rate and death rate as described, we can evaluate:

b(a+)−r(a+)=d(a+)b(a+) - r(a+) = d(a+)⟹b(a+)−[r(a+)+δ]=(k1⋅k2)12c⋅D(a+)N(a+)\implies b(a+) - \Big[r(a+) + \delta \Big] = \frac{(k1 \cdot k2) ^ \frac{1}{2}}{c} \cdot \frac{D(a+)}{N(a+)}

⟹b(a+)−r(a+)= intercept + slope ⋅D(a+)N(a+) \implies b(a+) - r(a+) = \text{ intercept } + \text{ slope } \cdot \frac{D(a+)}{N(a+)}

Where:

intercept =δ=1tln(k1k2)\text{intercept } = \delta = \frac{1}{t} \text{ln} \Big(\frac{k1}{k2} \Big)

slope =(k1⋅k2)12c\text{slope } = \frac{(k1 \cdot k2)^\frac{1}{2}}{c} At this point, the intercept and slope are the only unknowns, so this is a system we know how to solve. We use all values of aa within a chosen range (“age trim”), combined with orthogonal regression, to estimate slope and intercept. Orthogonal regression for y∼xy \sim x has an analytical solution as follows:

slope =sd(y)sd(x)\text{slope } = \frac{\text{sd}(y)}{\text{sd}(x)}

intercept =mean(y)−mean(x)⋅ slope \text{intercept } = \text{mean}(y) - \text{mean}(x) \cdot \text{ slope } Then, solve for completeness using slope, intercept, and the relationships above, as follows:

  1. Solve for relative census coverage: intercept =1tln(k1k2)\text{intercept } = \frac{1}{t} \text{ln} \Big(\frac{k1}{k2} \Big)⟹k1k2=exp(intercept⋅t)\implies {\frac{k1}{k2} = \text{exp}(\text{intercept} \cdot t)}

  2. Use k1k2\frac{k1}{k2} to select k1k1 and k2k2 assuming the more complete census is 100% complete

  3. Then: c=(k1⋅k2)12slopec = \frac{(k1 \cdot k2)^\frac{1}{2}}{\text{slope}}

Using this package for GGB

To use this package for GGB, use the ggb function:

results <- ggb(
  dt,
  age_trim_lower = 5,
  age_trim_upper = 85,
  id_cols = c("location", "sex", "age_start"),
  migration = FALSE,
  input_deaths_annual = TRUE
)

This will return a list of two objects. The first has your input data with GGB component columns added:

head(results[["dt"]])
#>        location    pop1    pop2    deaths  migrants age_start    sex      date1
#>          <char>   <num>   <num>     <num>     <num>     <num> <char>     <Date>

The second has completeness by each set of ID columns, as well as summaries such as slope, intercept, and relative census coverage:

print(results[["completeness"]])
#>        location    sex   slope    intercept completeness k1_over_k2
#>          <char> <char>   <num>        <num>        <num>      <num>
#> 1: South Africa   male 1.05593 -0.005452145    0.9333123  0.9712342

You can also plot the linear fit using the plot_ggb function:

id_cols_subset = list(
  location = "South Africa",
  sex = "male",
  age_start = seq(5, 80, 5)
)
gg <- plot_ggb(results, id_cols_subset = id_cols_subset)
print(gg)

In this plot, the x-axis is the incomplete death rate (D(a+)N(a+)\frac{D(a+)}{N(a+)}). The y-axis is the entry rate minus estimated growth rate, b(a+)−r(a+)b(a+)−r(a+). Each dot represents one age value, aa, and is labeled with that value. The slope and intercept of the trend line are the slope and intercept described above which are used to estimate completeness. This plot can be used to evaluate age-trim selection, based on outliers. Trends in residuals can also indicate potential error due to migration.
